steps.note: The program starts in main. The add_score machine waits on the right until somebody calls it.
main makes its own box called score and puts 0 in it.
Calling add_score(score, 10): a copy of score (0) and the number 10 go into the machine's slot.
Inside, score and points are the machine's own variables, holding what was passed in: 0 and 10.
total is made inside the machine: 0 + 10 is 10.
return hands total back. The 10 drops into the OUT tray.
The 10 comes out of the machine and lands in main's score. The machine's insides vanish.
Calling it again: a copy of the new score (10) and the number 5 go in.
A fresh score and points, this time 10 and 5.
total is 10 + 5, which is 15.
return drops the 15 into the tray.
15 comes out and lands in main's score, replacing 10.
printf prints main's score: 15.
return 0 ends the program.
Before running anything, the compiler reads this prototype and writes print_menu on its contents page.
A second entry: square takes an int and hands back an int.
Now main starts. Its two functions are written further down, but the contents page already lists them.
main calls print_menu. The compiler already allowed this, because the contents page listed it.
The call jumps down to the real print_menu. void and (void) match the contents entry.
Its one line runs: the menu prints.
print_menu is finished. It is void, so nothing comes back.
main calls square(4). The compiler already allowed this, because the contents page listed it.
The call jumps down to the real square. int and (int n) match its contents entry. n is 4.
n * n is 4 * 4, which is 16. return sends it back.
16 comes back to main and printf prints it.
return 0 ends the program.
The program starts in main, which is its own room.
Inside main's room, score is a box holding 99.
reset(score) builds a new room. A photocopy of 99 goes in. The original stays put.
Inside reset, score is a new variable holding the copy. Same name as main's, but a different box.
score = 0 scribbles on the copy only. Look left: main's score is still 99.
reset prints its own score: 0.
reset finishes and its room vanishes, copy and all.
Back in main, score is still 99. The change never left reset's room.
return 0 ends the program.
A sticky note: wherever MAX_SCORES appears, write 5 instead.
A second note for START_LIVES. Capitals tell you it's a constant.
Before compiling, both names are swapped for their numbers: START_LIVES becomes 3 and MAX_SCORES becomes 5. The compiler only ever sees the numbers.
The loop starts with i at 0. Is 0 < 5? Yes.
printf prints Slot 0.
i goes up to 1. Is 1 < 5? Yes, so round again.
printf prints Slot 1.
i goes up to 2. Is 2 < 5? Yes, so round again.
printf prints Slot 2.
i goes up to 3. Is 3 < 5? Yes, so round again.
printf prints Slot 3.
i goes up to 4. Is 4 < 5? Yes, so round again.
printf prints Slot 4.
i is 5. Is 5 < 5? No, so the loop is over. Five slots, from the one number on line 3.
printf prints lives, which is 3.
return 0 ends the program.
main starts. No lockers yet.
Five lockers in a row, numbered 0 to 4. The braces fill them in order.
The whole row is 20 bytes and one locker is 4 bytes. 20 / 4 = 5, so count is 5.
scores[0] is the first locker, not scores[1]. It holds 90.
scores[4] is the last locker (count - 1). Its 10 is replaced with 25.
i starts at 0. Is 0 < 5? Yes.
printf shows i + 1 and scores[i]: 1: 90.
i is 1. Is 1 < 5? Yes.
printf shows i + 1 and scores[i]: 2: 75.
i is 2. Is 2 < 5? Yes.
printf shows i + 1 and scores[i]: 3: 60.
i is 3. Is 3 < 5? Yes.
printf shows i + 1 and scores[i]: 4: 40.
i is 4. Is 4 < 5? Yes.
printf shows i + 1 and scores[i]: 5: 25.
i is 5. Is 5 < 5? No, the loop ends. There is no locker 5.
return 0 ends the program.
string.h is the string toolbox: strlen, strcmp and friends.
main starts.
Eight char lockers. Sam fills the first three, then C adds a stop sign, \0, in locker 3. The rest are zero too.
%s prints letters one by one until it hits the stop sign.
strlen counts the letters before the stop sign: 3.
sizeof counts every locker, used or not: 8.
A string is just lockers, so you can change one letter. Locker 1 becomes u.
Walking along again: S, u, m, then the stop sign. It reads Sum.
return 0 ends the program.

do.t: the stop sign decides where a string ends

steps.note: main starts.
name has 32 lockers (we can see the first 8). They hold leftover junk, shown as ?. One locker is kept for the stop sign.
The prompt appears.
fgets waits. Sample input: Sam, then Enter. It scoops the whole line into name, Enter (\n) included, and adds the stop sign.
fgets read a line, so it didn't return NULL. The check is false, and lines 8 and 9 are skipped.
Printing name shows [Sam. The Enter jumps to a new line, so the ] lands on the next line.
strcspn finds the first Enter: locker 3. Writing the stop sign there cuts the line short.
Now the string ends right after Sam, so the ] sits next to it.
return 0 ends the program.
main starts.
cmd holds q u i t, then the stop sign.
strcmp walks along both words together, letter against letter. Every pair matches, and both end together.
No difference means strcmp gives 0, so == 0 is true and the block runs.
The if block runs: Bye.
apple against banana: the very first letters already differ. a comes before b, so strcmp gives a negative number.
Is that negative number less than 0? Yes, so the comparison is true, which prints as 1.
Sam against sam: capital S is 83, small s is 115. They differ at the first letter, and S sorts earlier.
Not zero, so they don't match: == 0 is false, which prints as 0.
return 0 ends the program.
main starts. The map isn't built yet.
map[ROWS][COLS] is 3 rows of 5 tiles, all empty so far. Row number first, then column.
Row 0 is a wall of five #.
Row 1: wall, floor, the player P, floor, wall. P sits at column 2.
Row 2 is another wall.
map[1][3] is row 1, column 3: the floor right of P. It becomes E, the exit.
The outer loop picks row 0. r starts at 0.
The inner loop starts at column 0.
printf prints each tile as c goes 0 to 4. The loop repeats for every column.
The row is done, so print a newline.
The outer loop picks row 1.
The inner loop starts at column 0.
printf prints each tile as c goes 0 to 4. The loop repeats for every column.
The row is done, so print a newline.
The outer loop picks row 2.
The inner loop starts at column 0.
printf prints each tile as c goes 0 to 4. The loop repeats for every column.
The row is done, so print a newline.
r is 3. Is 3 < 3? No, so the outer loop ends.
return 0 ends the program.
This line only quiets a Microsoft warning. Nothing changes in the picture.
main starts. The notebook best.txt will live in the drawer called the disk.
fopen opens best.txt for writing. The notebook comes out with a fresh page, and f is the handle that points at it.
fopen worked, so f is not NULL. The check is false and we skip the error message.
fprintf writes 120 and a new line onto the page.
fclose saves the page and puts the notebook back in the drawer.
best starts at 0.
"r" opens the same notebook for reading. The 120 we wrote is still on the page.
f is not NULL, so the notebook opened fine and we go inside.
fscanf reads the number off the page and stores it in best.
fclose puts the notebook back.
printf prints best: 120, read back from the file.
return 0 ends the program.
Before main runs, the global wave is made and set to 1. So is spawned: static locals are made once, up front. The left box holds what lasts all game.
main calls spawn_enemy. Its room opens.
fresh is an ordinary local: a new box, set to 0.
spawned++ changes the long-lived box: 0 becomes 1.
fresh++ makes fresh 1.
printf reads the global wave, plus both counters.
The function ends. fresh is wiped. spawned stays, because it's static.

do.t: fresh is gone, spawned is kept

steps.note: Second call. A brand-new fresh starts at 0. spawned still holds 1.
Lines 7 to 9 ran again: spawned climbed to 2, fresh only reached 1.
The call has ended and fresh is wiped. Back in main, wave = 2 changes the global.
Third call. Another fresh at 0.
spawned reaches 3, fresh is 1 again, and spawn_enemy sees the new wave without being passed it.
return 0 ends the program. Only now do the global and the static go away.
main starts. No lockers yet.
Capacity 5: five lockers. Three get scores and the two left over start at 0.
count says how many lockers hold real scores: 3.
add_bonus(scores, count, 5): the function gets where the lockers are, not a copy of them, plus 3 and 5.

do.t: no copy: add_bonus opens main's lockers

steps.note: i is 0. Is 0 < 3? Yes.
scores[0] += 5 changes main's box 0: 40 becomes 45.
i is 1. Is 1 < 3? Yes.
scores[1] += 5 changes main's box 1: 95 becomes 100.
i is 2. Is 2 < 3? Yes.
scores[2] += 5: 60 becomes 65.
i is 3. Is 3 < 3? No. The loop stops at count, so lockers 3 and 4 are never touched.

do.t: loops stop at count, not capacity

steps.note: print_scores reads the same lockers. They've changed, because add_bonus worked on main's array.
return 0 ends the program.
main starts.
typed holds the name the player gave: Alexandra, 9 letters.
name gets NAME_MAX + 1 boxes: 9. They hold leftover junk for now, shown as ?.
line has 32 boxes. It's used later, for joining.
snprintf copies letter by letter. After 8 letters only one box is left, and it's kept for the stop sign. The final a never goes in.
snprintf returns 9: how long the whole name would have been. That goes into need.
%s walks along to the stop sign: Alexandr.
need >= 9 is 9 >= 9: true. The return value is how you know the name was cut.
The warning prints the length snprintf wanted.
Joining: name, " scored " and 4500 go into line in one call. 20 letters plus the stop sign fit in 32 boxes, so nothing is cut.
line is an ordinary string, so %s prints it.
return 0 ends the program.

do.t: snprintf: never past the size, always a stop sign
